Examining annual payroll efficiency scores reveals important differences in how the four organizations achieved their six-year averages. The Tampa Bay Rays exhibited substantial fluctuations, with particularly strong efficiency scores in 2021 and 2023 contributing to their leading six-year average of 0.1220. Despite exceeding the leaguewide win average in only four of six seasons, Tampa Bay ranked first overall, demonstrating how exceptional individual seasons can influence long-term efficiency rankings.

In contrast, the Milwaukee Brewers demonstrated greater consistency, maintaining positive efficiency scores throughout all six seasons while experiencing an upward trajectory from 2024 to 2026. Although their average efficiency score of 0.1180 was marginally lower than Tampa Bay's, Milwaukee's sustained and improving performance suggests a more consistent pattern of payroll-adjusted success. The Los Angeles Dodgers exhibited a different trend, maintaining positive efficiency scores despite substantial expenditure but experiencing a general decline in efficiency over the period examined. Meanwhile, the New York Mets recorded considerably lower and less consistent efficiency scores, averaging just 0.0088 despite maintaining one of the highest payrolls among the selected organizations.

These findings demonstrate that similar average efficiency rankings can conceal differences in annual performance and consistency. While Tampa Bay benefited from particularly strong individual seasons, Milwaukee demonstrated sustained success, and the Dodgers illustrated that high expenditure can coexist with favourable efficiency. Consequently, evaluating organizational efficiency requires examining annual trajectories alongside average scores, particularly given the sensitivity of the index to payroll expenditure.

### Impact of Alternative Salary Cap and Payroll Floor Structures

To examine how alternative salary cap-and-floor structures would affect organizations with contrasting financial and competitive characteristics, the three scenarios developed in Section 5 were applied to the 2026 payrolls of the four selected franchises. Table 15 presents each organization's payroll status and the minimum adjustment required under each scenario.

```{r section-6-cap-data, include=FALSE}
# Select 2026 payroll data for the four case-study teams
payroll_data_6C <- payroll_data_6A %>%
  dplyr::filter(year == 2026) %>%
  dplyr::select(team, year, `team payroll`)

# Apply the three salary cap-and-floor scenarios
payroll_data_6D <- tidyr::crossing(
  payroll_data_6C,
  salary_scenarios
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    payroll_status = dplyr::case_when(
      `team payroll` > salary_cap ~ "Above Cap",
      `team payroll` < salary_floor ~ "Below Floor",
      TRUE ~ "Within Range"
    ),
    required_adjustment = dplyr::case_when(
      `team payroll` > salary_cap ~ salary_cap - `team payroll`,
      `team payroll` < salary_floor ~ salary_floor - `team payroll`,
      TRUE ~ 0
    )
  )
```


```{r section-6-cap-summary, include=FALSE}
payroll_data_6E <- payroll_data_6D %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    payroll_2026 = `team payroll` / 1e6,
    adjustment_millions = required_adjustment / 1e6
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    team,
    scenario,
    payroll_2026,
    payroll_status,
    adjustment_millions
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(team, scenario)
```


```{r section-6-cap-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
table_6_cap <- payroll_data_6E %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    payroll_2026 = sprintf("$%.2fM", payroll_2026),
    adjustment_millions = ifelse(
      adjustment_millions < 0,
      paste0("-$", sprintf("%.2f", abs(adjustment_millions)), "M"),
      paste0("$", sprintf("%.2f", adjustment_millions), "M")
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  table_6_cap,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "l", "r"),
  col.names = c(
    "Organization",
    "Scenario",
    "2026 Payroll",
    "Status",
    "Adjustment"
  ),
  caption = paste(
    "Impact of Alternative Salary Cap and Payroll Floor",
    "Scenarios on Selected MLB Organizations (2026)"
  )
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center",
    font_size = 8
  )
```


Applying the three alternative salary cap-and-floor scenarios to the four selected organizations reveals substantial differences in how financial regulations would affect teams with contrasting payroll structures. The Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets exceeded the proposed salary caps under all three scenarios, requiring payroll reductions regardless of the regulatory structure. Under the restrictive Scenario B, the Dodgers would face a reduction of approximately $215.21 million, illustrating the magnitude of the adjustments required of MLB's highest-spending organizations.

Conversely, the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays would generally face requirements to increase payroll expenditure. Milwaukee fell below the minimum spending threshold under Scenarios A and B but remained within the permitted range under Scenario C. Tampa Bay, meanwhile, fell below the payroll floor in all three scenarios, requiring an increase of approximately $71.87 million under Scenario A. These findings demonstrate that salary cap-and-floor structures would affect organizations differently depending on their existing financial commitments.

Importantly, these hypothetical adjustments would be determined by payroll expenditure rather than organizational efficiency or competitive success. Despite their contrasting performance records, both the Dodgers and Mets would face spending restrictions, while Milwaukee and Tampa Bay would be required to increase expenditure under certain scenarios despite their favourable efficiency rankings. Although such structures would reduce differences in payroll expenditure, the analysis does not establish whether they would produce more balanced competitive outcomes.

## Discussion, Limitations, and Conclusions

### Discussion of Key Findings

The findings of this study suggest that while financial expenditure is associated with competitive success in Major League Baseball, payroll alone provides a limited explanation of regular-season performance. Across 180 team-season observations from 2021 to 2026, the relationship between payroll expenditure and regular-season victories was moderately positive (r = 0.3417), with payroll accounting for approximately 11.7% of the variation in wins under a simple linear regression model. Although higher-spending organizations generally demonstrated stronger performance, the relatively low explanatory power indicates that factors beyond payroll contribute substantially to differences in competitive outcomes.

This relationship became considerably weaker when examining year-over-year changes. The correlation between changes in payroll and changes in victories was slightly negative (r = -0.0778), with an R² of approximately 0.0061. These findings suggest that increases in expenditure were not consistently accompanied by improvements in regular-season performance during the period examined. Importantly, this does not establish that additional spending is ineffective, but rather that changes in payroll alone were insufficient to explain changes in team performance.

The payroll efficiency analysis provided further insight into the distinction between financial resources and competitive outcomes. The Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers achieved the highest six-year average efficiency scores, despite maintaining comparatively modest payrolls. However, their annual trajectories revealed different patterns. Tampa Bay's leading average reflected substantial fluctuations and particularly strong individual seasons, whereas Milwaukee demonstrated more consistent above-average performance and improving efficiency during the latter part of the period. The Los Angeles Dodgers also ranked favourably despite substantial expenditure, demonstrating that high payrolls and strong payroll-adjusted performance are not mutually exclusive.

The comparative organizational analysis further emphasized these differences. Despite maintaining similarly substantial payrolls, the Dodgers and New York Mets achieved markedly different competitive outcomes. In 2023, for example, the Mets maintained a higher payroll but recorded 25 fewer victories than the Dodgers. This contrast demonstrates that organizations with comparable financial resources do not necessarily achieve comparable results, reinforcing the limitations of expenditure as a standalone measure of competitive potential.

The alternative salary cap-and-floor simulations revealed that different regulatory structures could substantially reduce payroll inequality across the league. Under the three scenarios examined, the payroll Gini coefficient declined from its original value of 0.2360 to between 0.0676 and 0.1823. However, these simulations demonstrate changes in the distribution of financial expenditure rather than changes in competitive outcomes. Consequently, while salary restrictions and minimum spending requirements may reduce financial disparities between organizations, their potential effects on competitive balance cannot be established through the present analysis.

Taken together, these findings suggest that money provides organizations with financial resources that may support competitive success, but greater expenditure does not guarantee stronger performance or improvements from one season to the next. Furthermore, the distinction between financial inequality and competitive inequality is particularly important when evaluating potential leaguewide regulations. The results support examining organizational efficiency, performance consistency, and spending distribution alongside total payroll when assessing the relationship between financial resources and competitive outcomes in Major League Baseball.

### Limitations of the Study

Although this study provides insight into the relationship between payroll expenditure and competitive performance in Major League Baseball, several methodological limitations must be considered when interpreting its findings.

First, the analysis was restricted to the 2021–2026 seasons, representing 180 team-season observations. While this period captures recent trends in payroll expenditure and competitive performance, it does not necessarily reflect longer-term relationships across different economic environments or organizational cycles. Furthermore, the analysis treats regular-season victories as the primary measure of competitive success, excluding postseason performance and other indicators of organizational achievement.

Second, the statistical analyses primarily examine correlations and simple linear relationships between payroll expenditure and regular-season performance. These approaches do not account for potentially influential variables such as player development, injuries, roster construction, managerial decisions, or organizational strategy. Additionally, observations from the same franchise across multiple seasons are not fully independent, and leaguewide economic changes may influence payroll expenditure over time. Consequently, the reported relationships should be interpreted as descriptive associations rather than causal effects.

Third, the payroll efficiency index developed in this study presents several limitations. By measuring victories above the leaguewide average relative to payroll expenditure, the index emphasizes an organization's ability to exceed a competitive benchmark while accounting for financial resources. However, the measure is sensitive to the selection of this benchmark and may disproportionately reward lower-payroll organizations when they achieve above-average results. Similarly, organizations with substantial payrolls may receive lower efficiency scores despite achieving consistently strong competitive outcomes. Although the sensitivity analyses demonstrated that the rankings remained relatively stable under alternative aggregation methods, changes to the baseline produced meaningful differences in organizational rankings.

Finally, the salary cap-and-floor simulations represent hypothetical adjustments rather than predictions of organizational behaviour. The models assume that teams immediately adjust payroll expenditure to comply with the specified financial boundaries, without accounting for existing player contracts, collective bargaining restrictions, roster decisions, or changes in league revenue. Furthermore, the simulations measure changes in payroll inequality rather than competitive balance itself. As a result, reductions in the payroll Gini coefficient cannot be interpreted as evidence that implementing these structures would necessarily produce more evenly distributed victories.

Taken together, these limitations indicate that the study's findings are most appropriately understood as an examination of statistical relationships, organizational differences, and hypothetical financial structures. While the analysis identifies meaningful patterns in MLB payroll expenditure and competitive performance, additional research incorporating broader datasets and more comprehensive statistical models would be necessary to evaluate the underlying mechanisms responsible for these relationships.

### Implications for MLB's Competitive Balance

The findings of this study have important implications for discussions surrounding financial inequality and competitive balance in Major League Baseball. Although higher payroll expenditure was positively associated with regular-season victories, the relatively weak relationship suggests that differences in financial resources alone do not fully explain differences in competitive performance. Consequently, policies designed to reduce payroll inequality should not automatically be assumed to produce equivalent improvements in competitive balance.

The salary cap-and-floor simulations demonstrated that alternative financial structures could substantially reduce disparities in payroll expenditure across the league. However, the organizational comparisons suggest that the competitive implications of these changes may be more complicated. The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays achieved favourable efficiency rankings while operating with comparatively modest payrolls, whereas the Los Angeles Dodgers demonstrated sustained competitive success despite substantial expenditure. Conversely, the New York Mets illustrate that high spending does not necessarily produce similarly strong outcomes. These differences suggest that organizational performance cannot be evaluated solely through the amount of money committed to player salaries.

A salary floor could require lower-spending organizations to increase their financial commitments, potentially expanding the resources available for roster construction. Similarly, a salary cap could restrict the spending capacity of wealthier organizations and reduce financial disparities. Nevertheless, the findings do not establish whether these adjustments would translate into meaningful changes in victories. Organizations may differ in how effectively they allocate additional resources, while spending restrictions could affect roster construction and player retention in ways that are not captured by the present simulations.

These considerations highlight the importance of distinguishing between financial equality and competitive equality. A more evenly distributed payroll structure may address disparities in organizational spending power without necessarily producing a more evenly distributed set of competitive outcomes. Therefore, evaluating proposed financial regulations requires examining not only their effects on payroll distribution but also their potential implications for organizational decision-making, player allocation, and long-term competitive performance.

Ultimately, the results suggest that financial regulation may influence the conditions under which MLB organizations compete, but competitive success is shaped by factors beyond expenditure alone. Any assessment of salary cap-and-floor structures should therefore consider both their ability to reduce financial inequality and their potential effects on competitive balance, rather than treating these outcomes as interchangeable.

### Directions for Future Research

Future research could expand upon the findings of this study by incorporating additional seasons, organizational characteristics, and statistical methods to better understand the relationship between payroll expenditure and competitive performance in Major League Baseball.

One potential direction involves expanding the dataset beyond the 2021–2026 period. Examining a longer timeframe would allow researchers to investigate whether the relationships identified in this study remain consistent across different economic conditions, competitive cycles, and organizational strategies. Additionally, incorporating postseason performance could provide a broader understanding of organizational success beyond regular-season victories.

Further research could also investigate the factors that may explain why organizations with comparable payrolls achieve substantially different competitive outcomes. Variables such as player development, roster construction, injuries, and individual player performance could be incorporated into multiple regression or panel-data models. These approaches may provide greater explanatory power than payroll expenditure alone while accounting for differences between organizations and across seasons.

The payroll efficiency index developed in this study also presents opportunities for further refinement. Future analyses could examine alternative performance benchmarks, incorporate postseason outcomes, or compare the proposed index with established measures of organizational efficiency. Additionally, investigating the consistency and variability of annual efficiency scores could help distinguish organizations that sustain above-average performance from those whose rankings are influenced by exceptional individual seasons.

Finally, future research could extend the hypothetical salary cap-and-floor simulations by examining potential changes in competitive outcomes rather than payroll inequality alone. This could involve modelling how organizations might respond to spending restrictions, incorporating player contract structures, and exploring the potential redistribution of talent across the league. Such approaches would provide a more comprehensive assessment of whether reductions in financial inequality could contribute to greater competitive balance.

Together, these directions offer opportunities to move beyond the descriptive relationships identified in the present study toward a more detailed understanding of how financial resources, organizational decisions, and competitive outcomes interact in Major League Baseball.

### Conclusion

This study examined the relationship between payroll expenditure, competitive performance, and financial inequality in Major League Baseball from 2021 to 2026. Through correlation analysis, linear regression, payroll efficiency rankings, salary cap-and-floor simulations, and comparative organizational case studies, the research sought to address a central question: Does money buy wins?

The findings suggest that while financial expenditure is associated with regular-season success, its explanatory power is limited. Payroll accounted for approximately 11.7% of the variation in victories across the six-season period, while year-over-year changes in expenditure demonstrated virtually no linear relationship with changes in wins. These results indicate that although greater financial resources may provide competitive advantages, increased spending does not consistently translate into improved performance.

The organizational comparisons further illustrate this distinction. The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays achieved favourable payroll efficiency rankings despite maintaining comparatively modest financial commitments. Meanwhile, the Los Angeles Dodgers demonstrated that substantial expenditure can coexist with sustained competitive success and positive payroll efficiency. In contrast, the New York Mets illustrated how similarly substantial financial resources can produce considerably different competitive outcomes. Together, these organizations highlight the limitations of using payroll expenditure alone to evaluate organizational success.

Furthermore, the salary cap-and-floor simulations demonstrated that alternative financial structures could substantially reduce payroll inequality. However, reducing disparities in expenditure does not necessarily guarantee more balanced competitive outcomes, particularly given the differences in performance observed among organizations with comparable financial resources.

Ultimately, the answer to whether money buys wins is neither an unequivocal yes nor no. Financial resources appear to matter, but their relationship with competitive success is far from deterministic. The findings suggest that understanding success in Major League Baseball requires examining not only how much organizations spend, but also the competitive outcomes associated with that expenditure. Money may provide opportunities to win, but spending alone does not guarantee success.
